learn.b: Two programs can solve the same problem, but one may take a second and the other a year on big input. Big O describes how the number of steps grows as the input size n grows. We ignore the computer and constants, and look only at the growth.

O(1) is constant: the same work however big n is, like reading list[0]. O(n) is linear: a loop over all items. O(n^2) is quadratic: a loop inside a loop. O(log n) is logarithmic: the problem halves each step, like binary search. O(n log n) is typical for good sorting.

Count how many times the work repeats. One loop over n items is O(n). Two nested loops over n items is n times n, so O(n^2). Two loops one after another is n + n, which is still O(n). Drop constants and smaller terms.

Big O also measures space, meaning how much extra memory you use. Making a new list of size n is O(n) space. Often you can trade one for the other: a set uses extra memory but makes lookups O(1) instead of O(n).

lab.hint: Swap items[left] and items[right], then move them.
lab.solution:
def reverse_list(items):
    left, right = 0, len(items) - 1
    while left < right:
        items[left], items[right] = items[right], items[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return items

learn.b: A queue is like a line at a shop: new people join at the back and the first person is served first. This is FIFO. The two main operations are enqueue (add at the back) and dequeue (remove from the front).
Removing from the front of a Python list is O(n) because everything shifts. Use collections.deque, where append() adds to the back and popleft() removes from the front, both O(1).

learn.b: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. The last node points to None. You keep only the head, the first node, and reach the rest by following next.
To visit every node, start at the head and move with cur = cur.next until cur is None. There is no index, so reaching the item at position i takes O(i) steps, unlike an array where it is O(1).

learn.b: Adding a node at the head is O(1): make a new node whose next is the old head. Deleting after a known node is O(1): set node.next = node.next.next. Compared with arrays, no items need to shift, but finding a place costs O(n).

learn.b: Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version. Every recursive function needs a base case, which stops the recursion, and a recursive case, which moves toward the base case. Without a base case it never stops.
The factorial of n, written n!, is n times (n - 1)!, and 0! is 1. That fits recursion perfectly. factorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3), and so on, until factorial(0) returns 1.

Each call waits for the call it made, so Python keeps a stack of unfinished calls. When the base case returns, the calls finish one by one in reverse order. Very deep recursion overflows the stack, and Python stops at around 1000 calls.

Ask: what is the smallest case I can answer directly, and how can the big case use the answer to a smaller one? For the sum of a list: an empty list sums to 0, otherwise it is the first item plus the sum of the rest. Fibonacci calls itself twice, which can be slow, so use it only for small n.

learn.b: Sorted data is easier to search, compare and group. There are many sorting algorithms with different speed. In real Python code you use sorted() or list.sort(), which take O(n log n). Learning the classic algorithms teaches you how to think about speed.
Bubble sort walks through the list and swaps neighbors that are in the wrong order, so large values bubble to the end. Repeat until a full pass has no swaps. It is easy but slow: O(n^2).
Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. It is O(n log n) always, but needs O(n) extra space.

Quick sort picks a pivot, puts smaller items on the left and larger on the right, then sorts each side recursively. On average it is O(n log n) and very fast, but a bad pivot choice can make it O(n^2).

learn.b: Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by looking at the middle. If the target is smaller, search the left half, otherwise the right half. Each step halves the work, so it takes O(log n): a million items need only about 20 steps.

Keep two indexes, low and high. While low <= high, compute mid = (low + high) // 2. If items[mid] is the target, return mid. If it is too small, set low = mid + 1. If it is too big, set high = mid - 1. If the loop ends, return -1.

Binary search only works if the list is sorted. On unsorted data you must use linear search, O(n), which checks one by one. Sorting costs O(n log n), so sorting once pays off only if you search many times.

The halving idea works on any question where answers go from no to yes. For example, finding the integer square root of n: guess mid, check mid * mid against n, and halve the range. Python offers the bisect module for ready-made binary search.

learn.b: A tree is a set of nodes in a hierarchy. The top node is the root. Each node can have children, and a node without children is a leaf. A binary tree allows at most two children, called left and right. The height is the number of levels.

A binary search tree (BST) keeps order: every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in the right subtree is larger. To search, compare with the node and go left or right. On a balanced tree this is O(log n), but a tree that is a straight line takes O(n).
A traversal visits every node. In-order goes left, node, right, and on a BST it gives sorted values. Pre-order goes node, left, right. Post-order goes left, right, node. They are naturally recursive.

Level order visits row by row, using a queue. The height of a tree is 1 plus the larger height of its two children, and an empty tree has height 0. Recursion fits trees because each child is itself a smaller tree.

learn.b: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) joined by edges. It models maps, friendships and networks. Edges can be directed (one way) or undirected, and can carry weights. The easiest way to store a graph in Python is an adjacency list: a dict from each node to the list of its neighbors.

BFS explores the graph level by level: first the start, then its neighbors, then their neighbors. It uses a queue. Keep a visited set so you never visit a node twice. BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. It takes O(V + E).

DFS goes as deep as possible along one path, then backs up. It uses recursion (or a stack). Mark nodes visited when you enter them. It is great for finding connected parts, detecting cycles and exploring mazes. Also O(V + E).

Use BFS for shortest paths or the nearest thing, because it spreads outward evenly. Use DFS to explore everything along a path, like solving a maze or checking if two nodes are connected. The only real difference in code is a queue versus a stack.

qs.why: Queue gives level-by-level order.
